children.text: yenedaṃ svecchayā sarvaṃ māyayā mohitaṃ jagat
children.translated_text: Victorious is the unconquered, glorious Lord, the kāyastha,
by whose own will this whole world has been deluded by māyā.
There is the district of Kashmir, foremost among auspicious lands, adorned with circles of learned men,
which has shattered the pride of the abode of Akhaṇḍala.
In it, his enemies' valor was checked by the pillar of his mighty arm;
the glorious king <s>Ananta</s>, conqueror of <s>Bali</s>, was like <s>Trivikrama</s> himself.
When that discerning king had warded off afflictions from his subjects,
and evil officials had been reduced to a mere memory,
then, by a certain playful man, a crest-jewel of the clever,
preeminent in assemblies of the learned, some sympathetic person
was urged to compose, for laughter, the conduct of former kāyasthas;
and on that occasion he makes a mockery of misconduct.
Homage to the maker of māyā, who has fashioned the display of the whole world,
to the destroyer of <s>Pura</s>, who causes creation, preservation, and dissolution;
to you, all-pervading, birthless, without qualities, bearer of digits,
lord over all officials, eater of every kālakūṭa poison.
Long ago, when the demons had been slain by powerful <s>Viṣṇu</s>,
their house-accountant, distressed and possessed of deep renunciation,
went to the bank of the <s>Vaitaraṇī</s> and performed austerity for a thousand years,
eating only handfuls of his own urine, out of hatred for the gods.
Pleased, <s>Kali</s> himself, the giver of boons, came to him and said:
'Go, child, to the earth, for the destruction of all the gods.
With this striking weapon, a pen, given by me,
you will make all the gods have their lamps and flowers cut off, deprived of incense and clothing,
fallen from their temples, smeared with dust, crying 'alas, alas,' surrounded by dogs,
and longing for libations of water from devotees.

children.text: jagati brāhmaṇānāṃ ca vṛtticchede tvayā kṛte
children.translated_text: When you have cut off the livelihood of the brahmans in the world,
the gods in heaven will perish through the interruption of sacrifice; there is no doubt.
Because you wept in heaven when the demons were destroyed,

children.text: tasmāttvaṃ diviro nāma bhuvi khyāto bhaviṣyasi ||
children.translated_text: therefore you will be famous on earth by the name <s>Divira</s>.'
His ink, black and swallowing everything, covers all with darkness;
for him, full of every māyā, it always grants accomplishment of every aim.
In your lineage here there will arise demons in the form of diviras;
when they have gained power, this earth will no longer truly exist.
When <s>Kali</s>, whose mind was stained with sin, had spoken thus and vanished,
after a very long time that being descended to earth.
Then he was born on earth from a butcher, a striker of vulnerable spots,
in the wife <s>Kuddālikā</s>, vowed to uproot the world.
In his lineage were born sharp men who destroyed every livelihood,
harsh, friends to no one, wicked, and stealing everything.
Like doomsdays, they devoured everywhere whatever was stationary and moving;
their whole bodies were smeared with ink, as if embraced by Time.
Sunk low, soft, rigid, and suddenly rising up,
like excrement, they were kāyasthas, clerks who caused harm to bodies.
At the time of service they had many mouths, like greedy hunters, and many arms;
in deceit they had many māyās and many forms, enemies of the gods.
When cities, villages, towns, market-towns, and lands were pervaded by them,
at that time <s>Kali</s>, scratching the sky with his ink-smeared pen,
danced, scissors in hand, wearing birch-bark as his cloak.
The hosts of piśācas sang, 'This great demon, named <s>Bhastrākakṣya</s>, eater of everything,
has been born for the destruction of the world.'
By that divira, robber of gods and cutter-off of fodder, salt, and cow-grass,
abundant food and drink are consumed day and night.
Formerly, when blessed <s>Viṣṇu</s> strode over the three worlds,
<s>Dharma</s> became liquid and remains in the form of ink.
When that lord of kāyasthas, cutter-off of the regular and occasional rites
of gods, nāgas, and men, again strode over the three worlds,
<s>Kali</s> became liquid and remains in the form of ink;
as the <s>Gaṅgā</s> grants heaven, so this grants hell.
Tormented by famous villages, by fetters, and likewise by clubs,
he became afraid, took to renunciation, and became a great ascetic.
Then, when his suffering was broken, he abandoned the vow and went to a distant quarter;
after time had passed and he had been forgotten, he returned, skilled in birch-bark documents and indifferent to truth.
Gradually, through appointment over villages, in the city of the accountant-lord,
esteemed because of hypocrisy, he obtained household business by fate's decree.
By his cruel dependents, who lived by following him,
the wealthy earth was made wealthless by manifest thieves.
<s>Dambhadhvaja</s>, <s>Niṣprapañca</s>, <s>Lubdhaka</s>, <s>Kalamākara</s>,
<s>Sūcīmukha</s>, <s>Bhūrjagupta</s>, and unbearable <s>Mahīmaṇḍa</s>:
these seven officials, demon-incarnations through his greatness,

children.text: luṇṭhyā vadhyāśca pūjyā ye sarva ityavadanmadāt ||
children.translated_text: said in arrogance, 'All who deserve to be robbed and killed are to be honored.'
<s>Upatāpa</s>, <s>Vajrapāta</s>, <s>Parigha</s>, <s>Dvārabhañjaka</s>,
<s>Dhūmaketu</s>, <s>Kapimukha</s>, <s>Kukṣibheda</s>, and <s>Gṛholmuka</s>:
these eight piśācas of his, chief soldiers going before him,
wandered with staffs in hand for the destruction of the mortal world.
Surrounded by hundreds of servants, always engaged in the worship of removing hypocrisy,
he recites a hymn, crying 'alas!' with tear-filled eyes.
With charming speech that steals the mind, seeing and being seen,

children.text: hyaḥ kiyanto mayā dattāḥ prāyasthā vijayeśvare ||
children.translated_text: 'How many likely candidates did I give yesterday at <s>Vijayeśvara</s>?'
Victorious is <s>Parameśvara</s>, whose endless greatness is made manifest.
Let these seventy-three go forward above those who stood at the beginning.
He who is enlarged by the wealth of splendor, compassion, awakening, and supreme bliss,
in place of expiation, let the dead <s>bhaṭṭas</s> be dragged with ankle-bonds.
He whose greatness is illumined by learning, he, the unconquered one, is victorious.
Let the officials who make smoke without a dwelling go to the villages.
To him whose nature is all bliss, who is the cause of all auspiciousness,
after confiscating everything, let those who forbid punishment be put to death.
And homage to the <s>brahman</s> whose form is consciousness and who removes all affliction.
The oppressed people indeed flow out like seeds of bdellium.
Noisy with such hymns and having deafened everyone with bells,
after giving orders he quickly entered the assembly crowded with officials.
<s>Marīca</s>, occupying a place made famous by the misdeeds of the people,
saw from afar an official, a messenger for the business, coming toward him.
He had a Śiva-image stuck to his foot and was a wheel for driving out temple property,
with a raised cap arranged in divisions of very fine folds.
He wore a body-guarding garment soft to the touch and of the color of flax flowers,
covered with thick cotton cloth fragrant with jasmine and musk.
He had a golden triple-twisted ring placed on a finger of his hand,
and, from the sighing weariness of the long road, he made distortions on his face.
Seeing that informer, that <s>Bhāgavata</s>, approaching near him,
he rose with delight, took him by the hand, and seated him at his side.
Homage to those informers, by whose favor officials,
though far away, become endowed with a thousand ears and eyes.
He said: Having heard that you stand at the head of powerful men,
I have come from the temple as one who shows the path to the heap.
Whatever cloth, ornaments, jewels, and the like exist in the temples,
all that, without remainder, I shall make manifest to you.
At <s>Vijayeśvara</s>, <s>Vārāha</s>, <s>Mārtaṇḍa</s>, and the others,
through the increase of your fortune, there is a heap sufficient to nourish the unfed.
Fearless amid reproaches and without hesitation in sins,
let a very sharp guard be constantly appointed there.

children.text: sa cāsti bhuvi vikhyātaḥ kāyastho bhavatā samaḥ
children.translated_text: And there is on earth a <s>kāyastha</s> (scribe-official), famous and equal to you,
without money, without effort, and without any confiscation of all possessions.

children.text: brahmahatyā na gaṇyante govadheṣu kathaiva kā
children.translated_text: For him killings of Brahmins are not counted; what then is there to say about cow-slaughters?
Through devotion to his master, people are uprooted by him from the root.

children.text: anye 'pi santi sarvatra tadvidhastu na labhyate
children.translated_text: There are others too everywhere, but one of that sort is not obtained.

children.text: nītaḥ svajanako yena nidhanaṃ bandhane dhanī ||
children.translated_text: By him his own father, though wealthy, was brought to death in prison.

children.text: yadi nāma bhavatpuṇyaiḥ sa sameṣyati madgirā
children.translated_text: If, through your merits, he should come together with you at my word,
then know your own house to be a free mansion of treasures.
As he spoke thus repeatedly, placing counsel in his ear,
that very great man said: Bring him quickly.
Then, with two or three rapid comings and goings as an act of respect,
he brought that sinful guard, having made certain of him.
His neck was stiff and raised like a piece of wood, and his eyes were motionless and turned upward.
He wore a head-cloth and jacket of a jaundiced green hue.
With a great hanging belly, resembling an unclean hollow,
he was enveloped, as if by a cleft, by a house of flesh.
Of fierce arrogance and great anger, taking lives and admitting no remedy,
he was like a fever of combined humors, full of complications and heat.

children.text: sa mahāntaṃ samāsādya duḥsahaṃ daṃśanaṃ viṭam
children.translated_text: Having approached the great, unbearable, biting libertine,
he easily brought him under control and obtained many temples.
Then, with countless men in front like embodied hardships,
he went to perform the time of offering, surrounded all at once.
The people understood him thus: This moving <s>Hiraṇyākṣa</s>, remembering an old enmity,
has reached the gods in order to destroy them.
When the wealthy, fleeing in fear, had gone from the temple,
the undiminished residents of the temples approached him again.
When the great festival of plundering household vessels and the like had begun,
with soldiers busy breaking open bolted doors and panels,
there suddenly arose a pitiful sound of weeping
from housewives whose garments had been snatched away and from terrified children.
Then there came one whose gait stumbled with the great joy he had obtained after a long time,
thin, Saturn-like, dusty, his belly wounded by hunger.
His head-cloth had many holes, with its border-rags dangling,
and his dirt-smeared body-covering was sewn with a hundred little patches.
His waist was concealed by an old, worn-out cloth, its border held in place,
and the rogue was pained by dry sandals brought by begging.
Though penniless, the clerk was proud of the preparation of documents,
appointed by the guard, like a snake living on air.
His wife, with her hips covered by a fragment of worn-out cloth,
with the tip of her nose smeared with lampblack and with dangling clay earrings,
angry because her children were hungry, with her head covered by half a winnowing basket,
rose up with a hissing sound, scratching her buttocks again and again.
When her husband had at last obtained a position, she was delighted and, gathering things from here and there,
with damaged text mentioning cakes, incense, and the like, she worshiped <s>Gaṇādhipa</s>.
He too, attentively hearing the master's many messages about wealth,
with hand extended for payments, wrote the documents without stumbling.
Shrill with the screech of his running pen, like a monkey being struck,
he quickly counted the dinars and produced two hundred documents.
whatever was useful for the feet of the guard.
a ladle, a wicker seat, a small mat, a pot, a vessel, and a little basket,
by making written grants of such things he reached the highest renown.
Before long he became prosperous, with full hands, arrogant with intoxication.
As he read out the written documents, his eyes rolling about,
he made all sorts of grimaces with various contractions of his brows and eyes.
Then, under the arrangement that the middleman's umbrella had been seized and broken,
the gambling clerk came, summoned by <s>Bhaṭṭa Bhāgavata</s>.
Proud from having nearly acquired the insignia of villainy, he had abandoned his rags;
the placing of a head-cloth had whitened half the surface of his forehead.
He was intent on gathering together the whole mass of villages belonging to every temple,
a protector who had reduced all the gods' guardians to mere ropes, as the corrupt text seems to say.
On arriving, he granted a long calculation of six autumn months,
within which there was written an amount of four and a half lakhs.
Then, when asked by him about a means for his own advantage under an agreement of acceptance,
he spoke, having assumed a little sincerity because he was pleased with his share.
In this temple, those well-known guardians of yours
have sold all their own property and gone away as my opponents.
But today I must do you a favor out of affection,
for that blessed family preceptor alone is the guru of us both.
Here, by accepting gifts together with five or six <s>cakrikā</s>-Śaivas,
all the property of the god is enjoyed, and so is the enjoyment belonging to the attendants.
Whatever remains unsold in the circle of the gods,
all that, by his very opinion, is to be enjoyed by you as if it were your own.

children.text: tathā hi tāmrajaḥ pūrvaṃ mahān nīto ghaṭo mayā
children.translated_text: For example, earlier a great copper pot was taken away by me;
out of devotion, with a hundredth part of it a bell was made in the temple.

children.text: kālena ghaṇṭāṃ vikrīya tadaṃśena kṛtā ghaṭī
children.translated_text: In time I sold the bell, and with a portion of that a small pot was made;

children.text: krameṇa bhakṣitā sāpi kṛtā śeṣeṇa ghaṇṭikā ||
children.translated_text: that too was gradually consumed, and with what remained a little bell was made.
That too was long ground down, and a tiny jingling trinket was made;
doing thus, a small remnant of the bell was preserved.
In this way, by Śiva-worship, a four-armed plunder is carried out.
There are thousands of measures of grain; let your honor here
perform what is called buying-and-selling, and then I shall make a report for you.
With these and those hundreds of devices spoken by him,
the guardian made the temple empty, like a walnut gnawed by an old mouse.
Then, inclined toward another accumulation and skilled in plundering good men,
the man versed in appointments obtained from him the village called <s>Āpatpraśamana</s>.
In his house, inside a great <s>Raurava</s> hell covered with sweepings,
whose great treasure was a water-pot with its nose broken and split,
where the rotten door strung with cords made a stumbling khaḍakhaḍa sound,
his dwelling had been in a house like the hollow of a hen-coop.
With a burnt blanket-fragment made into a head-covering,
lame as he walked slowly in old, torn sandals whose tips had been eaten by dogs,
with rags, sesame, clay, darbha grass, ritual rings, argha-vessels,
he carried a wooden bowl, full, broken, and torn by mice.
Bathing, muttering prayers, his beard bristling up, established in the path of good conduct,
he would go to the temple and recite a hymn for half the day.
Circumambulating cows, bowing to Brahmins, observing the twelfth-day fast,
he carefully gave one cowrie to a poor man on the road.
For that same man, by fate, when business came to him as an appointed official,
his house soon became filled with utensils, vessels, and the like.
Neighbors who in winter would not give him even charcoal
unasked gave him the clothes and ornaments he desired.
Then his house, whitewashed with lime and with its courtyard swept clean,
became full of many servants, like a temple with a vermilion-red interior.
His young wife, with a fine complexion of new loveliness produced by sweet food,
within days became equal to an apsaras.
After that, as he set out for the village, bedding, baskets, and the like
went out in front: an umbrella, a water-pot, a copper basin,
a spear, a falling seizure-device, a bell, a copper vessel, sandals,
a small elephant-goad, sacred footprints, a birch-bark bag, then ladles for offering,
a rosary, an ink-vessel, a mirror, a bathing cloth,
boxes, little packets, swords, sandals, and a mantra-book,
an astrological almanac, a sword-blade, a red blanket,
a sacred thread, a string, a needle, a pen, and scissors,
sweet flag, a lac amulet, a razor, a yoga-strap,
hymns and mantras, Ganges clay, bilva leaves, and a board for leftovers.
Having all been gathered together, this equipment and baggage went before him,
brought from here and there by a mind not intending to give it back.
With the creeper-like hand raised high, with a horse brought by hired men,
with jangling sounds and blows of the heel, while his mouth repeatedly bent upward,
as if threatening the people, as if making something unclear from the corrupt reading,
he went leaping toward the city, his thick garment hanging loose.
Then he entered the village, wearing a well-washed white rag,
like an old crane come for the destruction of village fish.
Then, under pretexts such as meals and daily observances,
thousands of hoards came before him as before <s>Yakṣeśvara</s>.
A yogin in thoughts of seizure, an expert in applying birch-bark documents,
separated from his own wives, enjoying the wealth of hell,
of no use in producing fruit, but solely industrious in fault,

children.text: aśokaḥ satataṃ rogī niyogī jayati prabhuḥ ||
children.translated_text: the sorrowless, constantly diseased appointed officer triumphs as a lord.
In thousands of climbs onto trees, and in hundreds of men generally exhausted,
in his village, when people had fallen into ruin, it became like hell.
He who, as a penalty for cows, imposed imprisonment lasting until death,

children.text: kā nāma gaṇanā tasya nṛṣu sarvāparādhiṣu ||
children.translated_text: what reckoning could there possibly be of him among men guilty of every offense?
Confiscation of all property, imprisonment, coercion, and breaking into houses:

children.text: iti tasya mukhādghoraṃ na cacāla vacaḥ sadā ||
children.translated_text: such terrible words never ceased from his mouth.

children.text: pañcaṣāḥ satataṃ tasya karabhā iva bhārikāḥ
children.translated_text: Five or six men, like load-bearing camels, constantly carried for him
ghee, honey, dinars, pepper, fresh ginger, and rock-salt,
beans, blankets, peacocks, shoes, sheep, and birds,
lotus-stalks, grapes, jars of honey, walnuts, couches, and stools,
bronze, copper, iron, and various household utensils and the like;
without resting, they carried home whatever he mentioned in speech.
And the warrants for penalties and dismissals which had come to him from his master
he tore to pieces with his nails, with contempt and spitting.
Though he always ate meat and ghee when the king's officer was present,
out of hypocrisy, when alone, he ate two handfuls of mung beans without salt.
Having got rid of the chief scribe, who was no healer of thefts,
he then made the watchman, supremely skilled in cures, his replacement.
Released by him from a twelve-year imprisonment,
that man, skilled in clear letters, quickly wrote a forged deceitful document.

children.text: kṛttāṅguṣṭhaḥ sa vāmena pāṇinā diviro rahaḥ
children.translated_text: The scribe, whose thumb had been cut off, secretly with his left hand
went to the rogue's house and made an arrangement on birch-bark.
Taking a jar of liquor between his two knees,
he repeatedly drank a measured amount, slowly becoming much more drunk.
With a pen-stroke high-pitched from the screeching sound of the reed, he wrote,
with his little finger, noisily, making the letters swell with saliva.
Plundering the regular and occasional expenses for Brahmins, cows, and gods,
he wrote what had been spoken by the glorious leather-worker guru, the sick master.
Again and again he sang, in a rough voice, a cry filled with devotion to <s>Śiva</s>,
while crushing lice with the tip of his nail after repeatedly picking them from his blanket.
Again and again sighing, and sighing once more, he denounced the activities of worldly life;
and, full of joy, he balanced the entry with the expenditure.
As if possessed by a <s>vetāla</s>, he trembled, dizzy with liquor,
adorned with a garland-like bracelet of bangles mixed with oozing paste.
He was absorbed in the pleasure of the loud music made by the flapping of thick birch-bark,
while his two dangling testicles came out through holes in his ragged loincloth.
His body was spattered by splashes from a full ink-pot rolling about;
drunk, naked, with stool and pot broken, the scribe danced.
Gray and with limbs smeared in filth, rising up like a demon,
he rejoiced, filled with intoxication, at the theft of people's livelihoods.
For a long time, in solitude, there was for him a strange pleasure of shoulder-music,
making a clanging sound from the striking and rubbing of his armpits.
Though the forest of people was constantly worked upon by that thieving scribe,
it blazed up together with him, like fire with wind.
Then, before long, when great wealth had arisen in his house,
adorned, garlanded, and vowed to chewing betel leaves,
his wife, intent on the mirror and looking out at the royal road,
though without him, displayed the pride of a king's mistress.

children.text: hāro bhārāyate hematāṭaṅkaṃ me na vallabham
children.translated_text: 'A necklace is a burden; a gold earring is not dear to me;
away with the heavy gold cord fit for a merchant's wife!
Only a single string of pearls is lovely; this delicate one is dear to me.'

children.text: iti darpagirā tasyā nābhavat kasya vismayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: At her proud speech like this, who was not amazed?
'Ah, blessed ink, bestower of success in every undertaking!
Ah, the pen, a certain mighty one, the abode of fortune!
She who once drank raw gruel begged for in a broken, sewn-up stone vessel,
by that very same thing now drinks musk-scented honey from a silver cup.'
Looking down at the beautiful <s>kāyastha</s> woman in the mansion,
the noble daughters of the neighboring houses sang thus.
She too, fawn-eyed like a young deer, under the force of youth,
as though split open by pride, did not look at the ground.
Hostile to the people of her mother-in-law's household, that young neighbor woman
was fond of joking talk and attached to song and instrumental music.
Her body anointed with lovely fragrance, she did not take up a bodice,
showing the expanse of her breasts, with the cloth over her head half slipped down.
Yawning, turning away, and casting her eyes sideways,
the restless-eyed woman looked at people, her creeper-like triple fold bending.
Seeing that graceful-eyed woman as easily attainable without effort,
libertines wandered near her house, coming and going with no business.
For a long time, desiring her, adorned with colorful garments, dress, and ornaments,
they spent money on fragrant oils, betel, incense, and the like.
Their hopes fixed on the official's wealth, eager to obtain that jewel of a woman,
they performed hundreds of gestures such as smiling and contracting their eyes.
Their tracks were not recognized even by those who knew them; they watched for an opening,
those snakes eager to bite, moving crookedly in play.
Going to an empty temple, two or three famous adulterers
considered a means of union with that neighbor woman.
One libertine there said: 'She is easy to get; there is no doubt.

children.text: khalvāṭaṃ tundilaṃ vṛddhaṃ svapatiṃ sahate katham ||
children.translated_text: How can she endure her own husband, bald, pot-bellied, and old,
always away from home, greedy, jealous, and incapable in love,
smelling with the rut-stench of a drunken goat, spitting thickly, and deceitful?
For a barren woman obstructed by a son, she has neither hope through him nor loss of youth.'

children.text: na ca duḥkhābhibhūtāsau rāgadagdhā na lakṣyate ||
children.translated_text: And, though overwhelmed by suffering and burned by passion, she is not noticed.
For by these faults even women of bad conduct do not come over.
Another said, 'You have considered the matter with good intention,
but effort must be made through nearness and acquaintance.
Without weddings, sacrifices, pilgrimages, divine processions, festivals, and the like,
no acquaintance is obtained for creeping near another man's wife.
Long gazing, repeatedly tossing up the restless locks,
stories connected with her and made under pretexts, and the display of generosity,
the establishing of a reputation for enjoyment, good fortune, and fame,
soft, soft speech in private, and respectful listening to her words,
placing one's eyes on her face, kissing and embracing a child,
the accomplishment of crafts for her, and looking at her clothes and ornaments,
when acquaintance has arisen, the offering of garlands, betel, and the like,
pressing her tightly against a wall and kissing her in a secluded place,
secret touching and intercourse: these are the devices for destroying chastity.

children.text: itthaṃ kā nāma na mayā kṛtā śīlaparāṅmukhī ||
children.translated_text: In this way what woman, turned away from chastity, has not been made so by me?
The wife of a niyogin is surely obtainable, always inclined to going out.'
Then a third also said, 'Everything is indeed under our control,
but here an obstacle is perceived because fate is unfavorable.
This one here, with a sharp-eyed file of papers, behaving like <s>Citragupta</s>,
a pitiless death-dealer who causes terror to the life of everyone,
by devices such as load-bearing, unrestrained toil, and broken records,
has reduced pitiless men to the condition of cowherds and keepers of cattle.

children.text: na kālo yadi nāmāsau tat kiṃ jīvanahṛnnṛṇām
children.translated_text: If he is not Time itself, then why is he the taker of men's lives?
If the damaged text speaks of sides or factions, why then is he the destroyer of one woman?
Asking again and again, "How many have died today, and where?",
that one, living off the dead and dog-like, observes a skull-bearer's vow.
With his hand raised to seize even the livelihood of good men,
we, full of faults, offer a handful of sesame and water to hell for him.
Although he desires his daughter-in-law and is the ornament of the Kalyapāla family,
still everyone is all-knowing when it comes to seeing another's faults.
Or rather, I have a powerful friend, beloved of the king;
by a mere word he will protect all our life.
Many burners of houses, killers of cows, women, children, and Brahmins,
mere servants of rumor from the quarters, have been protected by him.
This nun constantly enters with complete confidence
the house of the niyogin's beloved: a procuress, a <s>Vajrayoginī</s>.
She is the mother of spells for subduing, the accomplished go-between of lovers,
and the covenant-deity of women in initiations for obtaining men.
She would quickly deceive even <s>Arundhatī</s> in play;

children.text: purāṇapuṃścalī sā hi jāhnavīṃ manyate tṛṇam ||
children.translated_text: for that old whore thinks the <s>Jāhnavī</s> is mere straw.
She will accomplish what we desire before long.'
Having spoken thus, those rogues went to the house of the old nun.
That very doe-eyed woman in the mansion,
at one time with limbs filled by charitable meals, at another time with youth seemingly returned,
with a broad mark of burnt sandal-paste, wearing a large topknot,
proud because of the slow, low sound of his peacock sandals,

Then those men entered, bound by the time of initiation,
their eyes covered with cloth, as if blinded by false delusion.
Then the market-ascetic, placing his knees on the ground and joining his hands,
made a request to the guru, that inner chamber purified by faith, on behalf of the official.

children.text: ihaiva suciraṃ nātha yāgavyagre tvayi sthite
children.translated_text: Here, lord, while you have long remained occupied with the sacrificial rite,
other disciples are waiting, eager for the festival of sacrifice.

children.text: ya eṣa prathito loke gṛhakṛtye mahattamaḥ
children.translated_text: This very great man in household business, famous in the world,
who has begun the performance of sacrifice, is looking for you.
Whatever countless sin he has, such as brahmin-murder and the rest,
has been removed by you merely with the ringing sound of a single bell.
He regards all sin that destroys everything as mere straw,

children.text: yato mūrdhni tvayā hastastasya pañcaphaṇo dhṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: because your hand, like a five-hooded serpent, has been placed upon his head.
By your favor he has reached some extraordinary state, having crossed beyond;
for, though a Śaiva, he has stolen everything even from the temples of <s>Śaṅkara</s>.
The taking of all property, righteous good work, and the destruction of Brahmins,
all that belongs to that undivided man is only your own expansion.
Thus the very great man of household business, or the maker of his own desire for rubbing,
and this courtesan, lord, have come to invite you.
Let the installation of the ghaṭī-vessel be performed in her house, lover of disciples.
By the powders of subjugation that you have constantly supplied,
those wealthy lovers of hers have been reduced to mere bones.
With oaths by the treasure of the cremation ground, her tongue, hands, and lips worn thin,
this woman who moves under the guise of lovers is protected by your protective charm.

children.text: tailonmṛṣṭe manāksneho vadane na tu cakṣuṣi
children.translated_text: On a face rubbed with oil there is a little affection, but not in the eyes;
a prostitute has constraint toward men whose wealth is exhausted, not toward outcastes.

children.text: yadi sadbhāvinī vaiśyā yadi kālaḥ kṛpāparaḥ
children.translated_text: If a merchant woman is truly sincere, if time is full of pity,
and if a kāyastha is not a thief, then a prostitute too is affectionate.
This eye-doctor has arrived, an ascetic who is a refuge for all.
by whom the whole world has been made blind with filaments of saffron.
Because of the great abundance of eye disease in summer, when the fruit of autumn has attached itself to him,
let a complete sacrifice be performed, uninterrupted with pale creepers.
This barber is a remover of arrows for men, and by living from him
their testicles have been brought, by bad poultices, to the size of large pots.
By him, desiring shaven heads, <s>Cāmuṇḍā</s> had formerly been installed;
that man seeks from you a sacrifice for her annual day.
The wise man who, for a great price, for the joining of a nose,
even cuts off a lump of flesh and gives it from his own wife's private part.
And this old merchant, whose wife is young and who has great wealth,
because of poverty of power in intercourse, desires an aphrodisiac.
How can a young woman enjoy herself with an old man who is drooling, whose eyes are running,
who has asthma and cough, and whose penis hangs loose and slack?
Even when mounted in sex with effort, his standard ruined in its rising,
the old man gets no sleep, like a debtor thinking of debt.
Though his penis is like a squeezed intestine, he is eager for sex;

children.text: hastaṃ dattvā bhage vṛddho nidhānamiva rakṣati ||
children.translated_text: putting his hand on the vulva, the old man guards it as if it were a treasure.
Having made a diet of meat, milk, and ghee in hope of sex,

children.text: rātrau vamati tatsarvaṃ bhajate vā viṣūcikām ||
children.translated_text: at night the old man vomits all of it, or falls into cholera.
Seeing, among people, for a moment at the madhuparka, a husband old as dry hide,

children.text: sajane taruṇī dṛṣṭvā hrītā yāti rasātalam ||
children.translated_text: the young woman, ashamed, goes down to the netherworld.
By this old merchant, with wealth urged on by an old libertine,
the bride has been constantly wearied, as if burned, by his smeared penis.
This very man has made the moment for devouring many deposits;
he is a field of filth from wealth, a daytime thief in a merchant's dwelling.
Crooked, a serpent of the Kali age, he dances in times of sickness,
selling unknown grass, wood, and the like under the names of medicines.
The old man, with unwinking eyes, looks from afar at his beloved, longing for a youth,
like a sick man looking at polished food.
Therefore, having taken up the flower-season rite, let it be performed with the perfection of mantras,
so that the passionate wife may become the wife of one who has obtained power.
When the guru, his eyebrows troubled with contortions, heard from the disciples
an invitation such as this, reported by him, he said, I shall do everything.
Then at the end of the day, after first setting out a large <s>Śiva</s>-waterpot,

children.text: guruṇā saha te śiṣyāḥ papurbhuktottaraṃ ciram ||
children.translated_text: those disciples, together with the guru, drank for a long time after eating.
All the official's women, and his friends and kinsmen,
vomited that leftover food into skull-bowls and drank it repeatedly.
Then one began to sing, another cried out loudly,
one staggered, another jumped about, making hissing sounds.
One, acting out an extreme derangement born of devotion,
stood motionless for a long time, as if he had attained the state of a corpse.
Another, adorned with swinging garlands and overwhelmed with intoxication,
embraced men by the neck and kissed women as well.

children.text: tataḥ kṣībo guruḥ kiṃcit svakāvyaṃ deśabhāṣayā
children.translated_text: Then the drunken guru, making music on a small drum,
sang a little poem of his own in the local language, loud with the sounds of lute and flute.
Then the guru, from delight, raised one arm with one hand,
and, slowly rising from his seat, danced with both.
Then the disciples rose up, roaring with loud laughter,
embracing the women, their waist-cloths slipping loose.
When midnight had slowly passed and the circle of lamps had gone out,
their great festival of the wheel of sex became without distinction.
At dawn the guru rose and, quickly receiving the water-pot,
did everything as if it had been done, having been invited by other disciples.
In times of fever, the earth is full of gold for physicians; in autumn, for officials;
and in the flower season, for gurus.
Then a man very close to the official entered, breathing heavily, trembling, as if bursting,
looking to each side.
He said, Tonight at midnight the chief of the household business,
after stealing much royal treasury-money, has gone off with his followers.
When he had slipped away without speaking, among the officials connected with him
a strange bustle of flight arose in every house.
Your master, his face burst open by slaps, was taken into custody by soldiers;
first, while dropping excrement, he was at least kept under guard.
Before your beard is plucked out and you too are bound and led away,
some policy must be carried out in this terrible fear of the king.

children.text: iti bruvāṇe tanmitre taiḥ śiṣyaiḥ sahite gurau
children.translated_text: As his friend was saying this, and the guru, together with those disciples,
departed quickly, the distressed official sighed and said:
Ah, because of the wickedness of time, how dreadful is the Kali age!
Good men have utterly perished; alas, <s>dharma</s> has set.
Having said this, just as he, with his followers, was making ready for flight,
he leaked urine from fear, and then soldiers arrived and surrounded him.

children.text: sa rājñā hṛtasarvasvaḥ praklinno bandhane ciram
children.translated_text: With all his property taken by the king, he remained wet for a long time in prison;
freed by the money of his sister, a prostitute, he came out from there.
Then, bereft of wealth, he became a mutterer of spells, an interpreter of dreams,
bowing to everyone, a flatterer, and a sweet speaker.
He who had once been swollen and stiff, an official resembling a phallus,
after falling from office became like an old scrotum.
For those who are always blinded by the intoxication of office and whose eyes are angry
it is the supreme collyrium, a bondage that produces purity of the eyes.
He who despises even venerable men when, distressed, they have fallen at his feet,
once deprived of office, worships their feet when they are smeared with excrement.

children.text: aho bata muhūrtena bhavanti na bhavanti ca
children.translated_text: Ah, indeed, in a single moment they exist and do not exist:
the fortunes of officials are as fickle as the flame from burning straw.
Then, when his wife had risen and gone away of her own accord, he, now penniless,
that abode of greed, wandered about the houses of his relatives, seeking a lump of food.
Harsh, emaciated, exceedingly filthy, wearing a patched and burnt rag,

children.text: piśāca iva duṣprekṣyo dinaireva babhūva saḥ ||
children.translated_text: in only a few days he became hard to look at, like a piśāca.
His buttocks, testicles, and belly were scorched by the heat of a little pot of chaff-fire;
to drive away the colic from wind, he had a cord tied around his knees.
His throat was choked and his belly arose from having swallowed the wealth of gods and Brahmins;
his belly was gaunt with hunger, his mouth dry, and he wandered after having fallen into a rubbish heap.
His knees and feet were eaten by dogs, streaming with abundant blood;
he found relief in balls of rice given in compassion, eating leftovers softened by pity.
From his half-burnt loincloth his two testicles, with their hair, protruded;
his head, shoulders, chest, and sides were smeared with ashes, and he had lost all shame.
Babbling and longing for sour gruel, he was given a cake by someone;
at a public water-place he was refused a drink by its keeper, who mistook him for a ḍomba.
In the cold season, his limbs were covered with straw from a menstruating woman;
in a quarrel with beggar-boys over taking a potsherd bowl,
his eyebrows, beard, and eyes were burned by a blow from a fire-vessel.
At funeral rites he was repeatedly beaten with clubs by caṇḍālas;
lying in mud, he cried out on the main roads to charity-houses and sacred places.
Then that lowest of men fell face downward into a channel of human excrement,
and, with his hips raised high, gave up his life.
Thus, through the austerity of poverty, he went to the state of being only bones;
that tormentor of men reached hell by himself, with his body intact.
In this way, when the fires that are officials have gradually been extinguished,
the people, freed from torment and made fortunate by contentment, rejoice.
Thus this <s>Narmamālā</s>, a discussion of the crooked conduct and misdeeds of the host of wicked officials, has been composed

children.text: api sujanavinodāyombhitā hāsyasiddhyai kathayati phalabhūtaṃ sarvalokopadeśam ||
children.translated_text: for the amusement of good people and opened for the accomplishment of laughter; it states, as its fruit, instruction for all people.
